items.title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
items.abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

items.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
items.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

items.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
items.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.

items.title: From cyberspeak to algorithmic newspeak: soft derogation and the ethics of AI-generated language
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines the ethical and epistemological implications of language generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lenses of speech act theory, conversational implicature and second-order cybernetics. LLMs are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs actively participate in shaping discourse in ways that carry consequences for meaning, responsibility and pluralism. Design/methodology/approach The paper introduces the concept of soft derogation to describe a form of linguistic exclusion, one that operates through euphemization, omission and the simulation of neutrality rather than overt offense. Such processes can subtly promote or suppress certain ideas, values or identities without transparent authorship or intention. The result is a shift toward an algorithmically generated form of newspeak, where expressive possibilities are narrowed through alignment protocols and safety layers. Findings Drawing on second-order cybernetics, the paper argues that ethical responsibility for AI-generated language is distributed across developers, deployers, institutional stakeholders and human interpreters. While users co-construct meaning within recursive socio-technical systems, the upstream actors who design alignment protocols, moderation layers and deployment conditions bear primary responsibility for the communicative environments they create. Originality/value Relatively little work has examined how the pertinent philosophical frameworks can illuminate forms of linguistic influence that operate through euphemization, omission and simulated neutrality. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how algorithmically generated language can shape discourse while appearing neutral.

items.title: From Detection to Investigation: A Survey of Foundation Models and Agents for Financial Fraud and Financial Crime
items.abstract: Foundation models are extending research on financial fraud and financial crime from isolated risk detection to document understanding, relational analysis, and investigative workflows. A gap nevertheless separates model outputs from candidate evidence and actionable conclusions. This survey examines advances in six families of foundation models: language, vision, speech, temporal, graph, and tabular models. It compares their roles and limitations along two dimensions: the risk-control lifecycle and the directness of the supporting evidence. Existing studies show that pretraining can support representation reuse and the processing of unstructured information, with direct validation in some financial tasks. Cross-modal identity binding, information availability over time, report faithfulness, and case-level benefits require separate evaluation. Evidence on investigative agents spans prototypes, controlled tasks, expert assessments, and industry disclosures, which establish different aspects of workflow feasibility, task performance, and user assessment. Establishing gains in investigative efficiency and reductions in financial losses requires case-level comparative evidence. We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

items.title: From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.

items.title: From sensing to transforming: The discursive trajectory of AI and the limited prominence of human-centered engagement themes
items.abstract: Background Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption transformed work structures after 2022, raising psychological safety concerns as efficiency priorities overshadow human-centered employee wellbeing. Objective This longitudinal study investigates how engagement is framed as a corporate communication strategy in Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 technology firms during early large-scale AI adoption (2022–2024). Methods Using IRaMuTeQ, 150 S&P 500 corporate reports (2022–2024) underwent Reinert's Descending Hierarchical Classification, Correspondence Factorial Analysis, and similarity network analysis, employing chi-square ( χ 2 ) marker filtering. Results Findings reveal a three-stage trajectory mapping onto dynamic capabilities: initial sensing (2022), platform seizing (2023), and process transformation (2024). However, human-centered engagement language (meaningfulness, safety, vigor) remained structurally marginalized, failing to form a stable lexical cluster and framing participation strictly through technical integration. Conclusions Public discourse serves as a proxy for enacting dynamic capabilities. Practically, HR leaders should prospectively audit AI communications to ensure technical efficiency narratives do not displace human-centered and psychological safety registers.

items.title: From Solvency to Dignity: Artificial Intelligence, Energy, and a New Social Pact
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence requires systematic reflection on the relationship between technological progress, collective responsibility and the dignity of the person, making a new social pact necessary. The article links dependence on fossil fuels to geopolitical imbalances, inflationary pressures and the ability of authoritarian regimes to support power policies, proposing international coordination, including at the UN, that reconciles energy security, climate protection and the transition to renewable sources and, in perspective, nuclear fusion. This analysis is accompanied by the criticism of an economy based exclusively on solvency, which excludes needs without adequate purchasing power from the production and distribution of essential goods. To combat poverty, inequality and vulnerability to war, an international agency capable of promoting socially useful work and coordinating the production and distribution of fundamental resources is envisaged. In this framework, artificial intelligence and robotics could contribute to the analysis of needs, the organization of work, agriculture, assistance and scientific research, as long as they remain subordinate to democratic decision-making and criteria of transparency, human control and non-discrimination. Finally, the technological comparison between the United States, China and Europe shows the need, especially for Europe, to strengthen investment, research and regulatory capacity. Energy, peace, social justice and innovation are thus brought back to the different dimensions of a single pact based on collective responsibility and human dignity.

items.title: From the Law of the Horse to the Workflow: Why Institutions, Not the Model, Decide the EU AI Act’s Effectiveness: Lessons from Hungary’s First-Wave Implementation
items.abstract: Abstract Whether a new technology needs its own law is an old question, and for artificial intelligence (AI), it has been posed at the wrong level of abstraction. Both the case against technology-specific law and the case for regulation by design treat the AI model as the regulated object, although a general-purpose model acquires its risk only when deployed. This article relocates the regulatory object to the deployment workflow, defined as the envelope of thresholds, escalation pathways and human checkpoints that surrounds a model in use, and reads the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as management-based regulation that works only where the workflow is specifiable and a standing supervisor examines it. Hungary’s first-wave implementation shows the second condition deciding the outcome: the same obligations are supervised by the central bank in finance and by a ministry with no examination relationship in employment, so the Act’s uniform text conceals uneven supervision within one Member State. The Digital Omnibus on AI, which postpones the high-risk obligations because standards and authorities are late, opens a window to build supervision deliberately: the priority is not better definitions but better supervision.

items.title: From Trajectories to Experience: A Survey of Experience-Driven LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents record in their trajectories which strategies failed and how they recovered, yet an agent that resolves a problem in one episode may repeat the same diagnostic detour in the next. Work on reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition addresses this gap under different names, making methods and their gains hard to compare. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task-execution trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies; it may be a trajectory kept as a precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We review methods through four lifecycle functions: formation selects or derives candidate experience from trajectories, organization makes it accessible, utilization applies it to current decisions or internalizes it into model parameters, and maintenance admits, consolidates, revises, and retires it as evidence accumulates. A recurring source of failure is guidance that loses its link to its applicability conditions and supporting evidence: it is over-generalized during formation, misapplied during utilization, and left unrevised during maintenance. We organize evaluation around intrinsic experience quality, the experience utilization process, and downstream effects, and separate three improvement claims: fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism. The reviewed studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Across seven application settings, we derive recommendations on whether reuse justifies its cost, what to retain, how strongly experience should influence a task, and when to revise it. We close with eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to correcting propagated errors and testing whether gains accumulate.

items.title: From workload to verified learning: reframing ECTS for AI-rich assessment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) weakens a practical assumption in the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS): that estimated student workload remains a credible proxy for learning when assessment evidence is interpretable. This conceptual article examines what follows when academic products are routinely produced through hybrid human–AI cognition. Drawing on Kane’s interpretation/use argument, assessment-security scholarship and recent work on GenAI in higher education, it reconstructs ECTS as an inferential system in which scores, generalisation, extrapolation and credit-awarding uses must all be warranted. The analysis shows that opaque take-home production can weaken each link: scoring may misread distributed authorship, generalisation becomes unstable, extrapolation to learning outcomes is less secure, and credit awards risk retaining administrative form without evidential force. The article proposes verified learning as a credit-level validity condition and specifies four safeguards: programme-level alignment, authentic transfer tasks, process visibility with declared AI use, and strategic controlled verification. It also identifies equity and governance conditions required for these safeguards to support, rather than undermine, comparability across ECTS-based institutions in AI-rich assessment environments. The contribution is to connect task-level assessment validity to credit legitimacy and to translate that connection into practical design and quality-assurance implications for European higher education policy.

items.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
items.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

items.title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
items.abstract: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

items.title: Gendered Perceptions and the Use of Generative AI in Academia: An Experimental Vignette Study
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.

items.title: Generative AI and Workforce Transformation: Developing an AI-HRM Framework for Employee Productivity in Deposit Money Banks Operating in Rivers State
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming the nature of work, employee roles and human resource management practices across organisations. Deposit Money Banks are particularly affected because their operations involve extensive information processing, customer interaction, documentation, decision support and knowledge-intensive activities. However, the extent to which Generative AI contributes to employee productivity may depend on how effectively organisations manage workforce transformation. This study examined the relationship between Generative AI and workforce transformation and proposed an AI-HRM framework for improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State. The study specifically examined the relationships between Generative AI and employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and employee productivity. A cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of selected Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State using a structured questionnaire. Reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. Out of 344 questionnaire administered, 300 usable copies were retrieved and use for the analysis with the aid of SPSS version 27.0. The findings suggest that Generative AI should not be viewed merely as a replacement for human labour but as a technology capable of augmenting employees’ capabilities and transforming the way work is organised and performed. The study therefore proposed an AI-HRM framework based on AI readiness, Generative AI adoption, employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and productivity improvement. The study concludes that Deposit Money Banks can achieve greater productivity benefits from Generative AI when its adoption is supported by appropriate HRM practices, continuous employee development and effective human–AI collaboration. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a context-specific AI-HRM framework for managing workforce transformation and improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State.

items.title: Generative AI in Everyday Academic Work: An Exploratory Survey of Usage Patterns, Perceived Effectiveness, and Concerns among Indonesian University Students
items.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but its educational value depends on how it is used. This conceptual article examines ways in which future teachers can use AI to ask questions, compare explanations, and check evidence rather than accept ready-made answers. A focused review of work on critical thinking, media literacy, and AI in education was used to build a practical teaching sequence. The analysis suggests that AI can support discussion and reflection when students first form their own view, check external sources, and explain their final decision. The article also describes risks such as confident errors and overreliance. The proposed sequence is a design recommendation, not a tested intervention.

items.title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
items.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.

items.title: Governing Epistemic Risk in Data-Driven Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework Integrating Data Governance, Platform Power, Algorithmic Governance and Information Integrity, with Application to Kenya
items.abstract: Data-driven decision-making increasingly depends on long socio-technical chains in which data is collected, integrated, modelled, ranked and circulated before it reaches a decision-maker. Existing governance instruments focus mainly on safety, rights and compliance, and existing scholarship treats data governance, platform power, algorithmic governance and information integrity as separate problems. As a result, the reliability and legitimacy of the knowledge on which decisions rest — their epistemic quality — remains largely ungoverned. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. Using an integrative literature review and a model-type conceptual design, it synthesises datafication theory, platform capitalism, algorithmic governance and social epistemology into a single data-to-decision lens. It contributes (i) a taxonomy of thirteen epistemic risks located along the data-to-decision lifecycle; (ii) the Epistemic Risk Governance Framework (ERGF), which maps four governance pillars onto six actionable governance dimensions; (iii) seven testable propositions, including a weakest-link principle of epistemic governance; and (iv) a comparative analysis showing where the ERGF extends the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the UNESCO Recommendation and Kenya’s emerging data and AI governance instruments. The framework is illustrated through Kenyan decision contexts and accompanied by a design science agenda for its empirical evaluation.

items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study undertook an experimental comparison of visual acquisition for the avoidance of Mid-Air Collisions (MAC) when using cueing provided by Head-Up Display (HUD) and Helmet-Mounted Display (HMD) symbology. BACKGROUND: Previous work has shown that providing accurate cueing can improve visual detection performance, but no study had quantified the impact of providing cues via a HMD to reduce MAC risk. METHOD: Military fast jet pilots flew two scenarios in a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation. In one, a HUD provided cues to nearby aircraft. In the other, a HMD was used alongside the HUD to provide cues. The study measured visual acquisition range of aircraft that posed a MAC risk, as well as subjective workload, Situation Awareness (SA), gaze direction, and qualitative feedback. RESULTS: Visual acquisition occurred at a longer range when HMD cues were available compared to using a HUD only. HMD cueing was associated with lower subjective workload and higher perceived SA. Participant gaze direction indicated that HMD cues resulted in a more focused visual search. CONCLUSION: Including HMD alongside the existing HUD used in military aircraft improved visual acquisition of MAC hazards, beyond that offered by HUD alone. The clear presentation of spatially referenced cues in the HMD enabled pilots to use a focused visual search process, improved SA and reduced workload.

items.title: Here is Why Artificial Intelligence Will Never Replace Mathematicians
items.abstract: The Question Everyone Is Forgetting OpenAI's release of more than 700 mathematical manuscripts has provoked an extraordinary question: is this the final nail in the coffin? Are mathematicians no longer needed? Mathematicians, and indeed the world, are so busy debating whether mathematicians will remain relevant now that artificial intelligence can apparently solve some of mathematics' hardest problems that everyone is overlooking a much more fundamental question: Who conceived those problems in the first place? Who decided that these were the questions worth asking? Understanding this is, I believe, the most essential part of the entire debate. The question is not who can perform the greatest number of successful mathematical operations. It is who gave mathematics its problems, and what is lost when the development of an answer is treated as disposable. I am concerned with the distinction between the final theorem, the proof establishing it, and the intellectual journeys through which new questions appear before that theorem has been reached. We celebrate the mathematician who solves a difficult problem. We award prizes for proofs, commemorate breakthroughs, and measure mathematical progress by the number and significance of problems resolved. But before any of these achievements became possible, someone had to conceive the question. Before a theorem could be proved, someone had to recognize that there was something worth proving. Before an equation could be solved, someone had to recognize that a relationship required mathematical expression. And before a field of mathematics could exist, human beings had to develop the intellectual appetite, intuition, and conceptual language that made its questions conceivable. This is not a minor preliminary step. It is the foundational act of mathematical creation. Consider the Navier–Stokes problem. Its mathematical formulation emerged from humanity's investigation of fluids, motion, physical forces, and the behavior of matter. The equations were not waiting in a computer as an arbitrary collection of symbols. They arose from human beings observing the world, attempting to understand it, and translating that encounter into mathematics. The same is true, in different ways, of the questions that gave rise to geometry, calculus, probability, topology, number theory, and the countless mathematical structures that followed. Even when mathematics eventually becomes so abstract that its connection to ordinary experience is almost impossible to recognize, its intellectual ancestry remains human. This matters precisely because we may be entering an era in which an AI system can deliver a proposed proof faster than a mathematical community can assimilate it. If we measure mathematical progress only by the answers delivered, the most consequential losses may escape our measurement altogether. The important question is therefore not simply whether AI can solve the Riemann hypothesis, the Navier–Stokes problem, or hundreds of other conjectures. It is whether solving questions conceived within the human mathematical enterprise is equivalent to possessing the intelligence, intuition, and origins of thought that created that enterprise. I argue that it is not. Solving a problem and being the kind of intelligence from which the problem was born are two fundamentally different accomplishments.

items.title: Hidden Microbiome of Mining Environments: Implications for Occupational Health, Bioaerosol Exposure, and Antimicrobial Resistance
items.abstract: Mining environments are extreme subsurface ecosystems characterized by elevated concentrations of metals and minerals, limited light, and high particulate loads. Occupational health research in mining has traditionally emphasized physical and chemical hazards, whereas biological exposures remain less well-characterized. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on mining-associated microbial communities, bioaerosols, occupational exposure, respiratory health, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The literature search covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception through August 2026. Evidence from coal, uranium, metal mining, acid mine drainage, and mine dust environments indicates that geochemical conditions and mining activities shape microbial communities. Drilling, blasting, excavation, and ore transport can aerosolize microbial cells, spores, and dust-associated microbial components, creating plausible inhalation pathways. Metal-rich environments may also favor persistence and co-selection of metal- and antibiotic-resistance determinants within environmental microbial communities. Metagenomic sequencing and environmental DNA approaches have expanded detection of microbial diversity, functional genes, and environmental resistomes. However, environmental detection does not establish microbial viability, effective worker exposure, transmission, or disease causation. Future research should integrate standardized environmental and personal microbial exposure measurements with respirable dust and chemical monitoring, longitudinal occupational epidemiology, and functional validation of resistance determinants to determine the actual occupational-health significance of mining-associated microbiomes.

items.title: How Does AI Literacy Relate to Pre-Service STEM Teachers’ AI Readiness? Insights from Mediational Analysis
items.abstract: Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

items.title: Human or AI-generated voiceover for chemotherapy education video? Evidence from knowledge and practice tests improvement among cancer patients by pharmacists
items.abstract: BackgroundEducational videos play a crucial role in enhancing healthcare delivery. Developing an educational video designed to improve patient understanding of catastrophic treatment. During the video's creation, two voiceover methods were employed: human voices and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated voices. To date, the impact of voice-over origin-whether human or AI-on patient knowledge acquisition remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study aimed to assess the differences in knowledge and practice scores among cancer patients exposed to educational video materials about chemotherapy, comparing human voice with AI-generated voice narrations.MethodsA total of 129 cancer patients participated in this study. Designed as a case-control study, participants were divided into three groups: a control group, a group receiving videos with human voice narrations, and a group receiving videos with AI-generated voice narrations. All participants completed a questionnaire assessing their understanding of chemotherapy. A three-group quantitative comparative analysis was conducted, focusing on topics such as administration procedures, treatment goals, and the management of adverse drug reactions.Key findingsBoth educational videos with human- and AI-generated voiceovers should be incorporated into the oncology healthcare system due to their effectiveness in improving understanding of treatment. Notably, educational videos featuring human-voice narration consistently enrich knowledge and attitude scores among cancer patients across all assessed chemotherapy topics.ConclusionThe educational videos, whether in human or AI voices, were effective in increasing cancer patients' knowledge and attitudes across all key topics. There was a sustained trend toward human-voice videos in knowledge and attitudes among cancer patients; therefore, the human educational video showed significant improvement in understanding of chemotherapy administration, goals, and adverse drug reactions. Although there was no difference between human and AI voice education, trends toward combining human voice with realistic scenario videos should be considered to facilitate deeper patient understanding.

items.title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation
items.abstract: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.

items.title: Humans and Machines: On the Ramp
items.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.

items.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
items.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence skill-up educational programme on youth unemployment mitigation for community development in Imo State
items.abstract: Youth are the largest active population of any nation, and they play substantial roles in achieving sustainable community development undertakings. However, some of the youth are underemployed, not in education, employment, or training (NEET). The study examined the impact of an artificial intelligence skill-up educational programme on mitigating youth unemployment for community development in Imo State. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, with a population of 6700 youth participants and a sample size of 469 selected using a proportionate sampling technique. The research instrument was a structured questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Skill-up Educational Programme Questionnaire (AISEPQ)”. Mean, standard deviation, and analysis of variance were used for data analysis. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence has increased youth confidence in competing for digital job opportunities, enabled them to access remote work and other digital employment opportunities more easily, given them a competitive advantage over other job seekers in the digital labour market, improved their chances of securing gainful employment that is directly aligned with the current job demands, and opened up employment opportunities that were previously unavailable. The study concludes that artificial intelligence boosted young people's confidence in pursuing digital job opportunities, facilitated their access to remote work and other digital employment options. It recommends that the Federal Ministry of Youth Development (FMYD), in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education (FME), sufficiently allocate resources for the transition period of the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions so that young people can meet the demands of a knowledge-based economy.

items.title: Impact of Expertise and Trust on AI-assisted Work
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents promise to extend what users can accomplish beyond their existing expertise, but they also raise the risk of producing plausible-looking work that users may struggle to evaluate. We ask how task-relevant expertise and trust in AI shape agent-assisted work. To isolate these factors, we conduct a think-aloud study in which 20 professionals with varying data-science expertise use the same agentic tool to complete the same data-science hiring assessment, used at a major U.S. company. We find that surface productivity can come at the expense of understanding: participants who delegated more completed more of the task, but were also more likely to produce invalid solutions. Experts more often resisted this tradeoff, sacrificing completion to decompose the task and scrutinize agent outputs. Our findings call for evaluating agentic assistance not only by how much it accomplishes, but by whether users remain able to evaluate the work they produce.

items.abstract: Background: Primary Health Care (PHC) performs duties for the network's orderly and care coordinator. However, its professionals are exposed to factors that influence the health-disease process, making it important to develop actions that reduce possible negative impacts on health. Aim: To report the experience of a resident physiotherapist in implementing a program focused on promoting the health and care of workers in a Family Health Strategy unit in Southern Bahia. Methods: This is a qualitative study, of the experience report type, developed between 2023 and 2024, within the Multiprofessional Residency Program in Family Health at the State University of Santa Cruz. The program, "Sextou do Trabalhador", was implemented in a Family Health Unit in Ilhéus (BA) and aimed at all professionals in the unit. Perceptions about the implementation were recorded in a field diary. Results: The program aimed to improve the health of primary healthcare workers using manual and instrumental myofascial release techniques, integrative and complementary health practices (music therapy and aromatherapy), as well as guidance on ergonomics and physical activity. High worker participation was observed, accompanied by reports of pain relief, stress reduction, and an increased sense of well-being. Conclusion: The "Sextou do Trabalhador" proved to be a viable and beneficial intervention strategy within the Family Health Strategy (ESF), promoting care, valuing worker health, and strengthening the role of physiotherapy in primary health care.

items.title: Individual dependency behavior in multimodal AI-assisted knowledge acquisition: influencing factors and explainable prediction
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to identify the key factors shaping individual dependency behavior in multimodal artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted knowledge acquisition and develops an interpretable prediction model to inform strategies for optimizing knowledge internalization. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Open, axial and selective coding of 32 semi-structured interviews yielded five factors: task execution, information processing, individual cognition, technology experience and knowledge management. Saturation Assessment Curve (SAC) confirmed theoretical saturation. Theoretical coverage reached over 97% by the 17th interview. An expert panel of 20 domain specialists reviewed the framework and confirmed satisfactory content validity indices (S-CVI/Ave > 0.80). Subsequently, 2,002 valid survey responses were analyzed using machine learning classification. A support vector machine (SVM) was selected for its superior accuracy and F1-score, and the Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) algorithm was applied to quantify feature contributions. Findings Task execution exerts the strongest influence on dependency behavior, reflecting individuals’ reliance on multimodal AI under task pressure and goal-driven conditions. Information processing and individual cognition positively contribute as secondary drivers, while technology experience and knowledge management contribute comparatively weakly. These results suggest that habitual, pressure-driven responses progressively outweigh careful, quality-oriented considerations in AI-assisted knowledge acquisition. Originality/value This study extends the theoretical understanding of dependency behavior in AI-mediated knowledge acquisition. It also offers empirical evidence to guide human–AI collaboration design, AI governance frameworks and sustainable knowledge management practices.

items.title: Individualized English Language Learning for Students with Disabilities through Adaptive Educational Technologies
items.abstract: The integration of adaptive educational technologies into language education creates new opportunities for providing individualized learning experiences for students with disabilities. Traditional approaches to English language teaching may not always adequately address the diverse cognitive, sensory, communicative and learning needs of such students. The development of flexible and accessible learning environments is therefore becoming increasingly important, particularly in home-based education. This study explores the potential of adaptive educational technologies for individualizing English language learning for students with disabilities. Particular attention is given to the adaptation of learning materials, instructional pace, task complexity, communication formats and assessment strategies. The study argues that digital resources, multimedia tools, interactive exercises, speech technologies and applications based on artificial intelligence can facilitate differentiated instruction and increase students’ engagement and autonomy. At the same time, technology should not be regarded as a substitute for pedagogical interaction. Its effectiveness depends largely on the teacher’s ability to select and adapt technological tools according to the learner’s individual educational needs. The findings suggest that a combination of individualized instruction and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more accessible, flexible and learner-centred approach to English language education.

items.title: Infiltrators on the payroll: the threat of fake North Korean IT workers and the exposure of Spanish organizations
items.abstract: North Korea runs a state network of IT workers who obtain remote jobs at foreign companies under false or stolen identities and channel their salaries to the agencies that fund its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. This intelligence report assesses the threat as of October 2026 and what it means for Spanish organizations. It draws on open institutional sources, including the joint alert issued by eleven countries on July 31, 2026, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team reports and U.S. Department of Justice cases, and it separates documented facts from analyst judgment. Generative AI has lowered the cost of fabricating credible identities, and local facilitators are the weakest link. No public incident has been verified in Spain, but the exposure factors match those of other European countries, and the likeliest entry route is a third party, not a direct employee (medium-low confidence). Defense therefore cannot rest on the cybersecurity team alone: it takes Human Resources, Security, Compliance, Legal Counsel and hiring managers working under one identity verification and insider risk model. The report closes with nine recommendations and a 180-day roadmap.

items.title: Initial Orbit Determination of Low-Earth-Orbiting Objects Using Multi-Site Space-Based Optical Observations
items.abstract: Space Situational Awareness (SSA) is a growing field of study which provides knowledge of Resident Space Objects (RSOs) to help maintain a safe and sustainable space environment around Earth. A primary component of SSA is obtaining Initial Orbit Determinations (IODs) of these objects via optical observations. The present way of obtaining optical observations is by using a single observation site. However, using only one observation site does not yield accurate range or IOD results. This research tests space-based single-site and multi-site observations of RSOs in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) to provide the necessary information to calculate IODs. Gooding’s algorithm is used to calculate IODs from the simulated data, since it is the most robust IOD algorithm discussed in the literature. The results from this research demonstrate that selected multi-site observations produce more accurate range and IOD results than single-site observations and, thus, provide advancement opportunities for various SSA efforts.

items.title: Innovative Practice and Exploration of Large-Model-Empowered Project-Based Teaching in Higher Vocational Education
items.abstract: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence represented by large language models, vocational education is encountering critical opportunities for teaching model transformation. At present, project‑based teaching for software technology majors in higher vocational colleges faces prominent challenges, including insufficient differentiated instruction, lack of personalized guidance, and disconnection between teaching content and industrial demands. Taking the course Fundamentals of HTML5 Application Development as a practical carrier and drawing on the reform practice of “Large Model + Smart Shipping” in our college, this paper systematically elaborates the implementation path of large‑model‑empowered project‑based teaching. This study proposes an innovative teaching mode integrating a three‑tier hierarchical project system, human‑AI collaborative learning guidance, and multi‑dimensional process‑oriented assessment. By constructing a course‑specific prompt library, a hierarchical project case library and an intelligent auxiliary evaluation system, full‑chain teaching empowerment of large models is realized throughout pre‑class, in‑class, after‑class and assessment phases. Practical results show that full‑process empowerment by large models can effectively address pain points such as inadequate hierarchical adaptation and shortage of personalized guidance in project‑based teaching. It provides a replicable practical paradigm for the digital and intelligent transformation of curriculum teaching for software technology majors in higher vocational colleges.

items.title: Intellectual Property Protection of Purely AI-Generated Content: Rethinking Authorship, Inventorship, and the Case for International Standards
items.abstract: The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

items.title: INTELLIGENT INFORMATION SYSTEMS FOR EDUCATIONAL MANAGEMENT: A FRAMEWORK FOR DATA-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING IN NIGERIAN COLLEGES OF EDUCATION
items.abstract: The increasing volume of digital information generated by Colleges of Education creates opportunities for evidence-based educational management, yet institutional data are often distributed across separate administrative systems and are not adequately transformed into actionable intelligence. This study developed an Intelligent Information Systems (IIS) framework for data-driven decision-making in Nigerian Colleges of Education. The study adopted a Design Science Research (DSR) approach, focusing on the identification of the educational-management problem, definition of system requirements, framework design, conceptual demonstration and evaluation. The proposed framework integrates institutional data sources, data integration and quality management, an institutional data repository, Business Intelligence and analytics, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, decision-support mechanisms, management dashboards, and governance, security and human oversight. The framework demonstrates how data relating to students, academic programmes, examinations, personnel, institutional resources and other administrative functions can be transformed from operational records into information and intelligent insights for management decisions. The study argues that integrating heterogeneous institutional data with appropriate analytical and intelligent technologies can strengthen evidence-based planning, monitoring, resource allocation, academic administration and institutional performance management. The framework also emphasises that Artificial Intelligence should complement rather than replace professional judgement, with privacy, security, data quality, transparency and human oversight incorporated into institutional implementation. The study contributes a Computer Science-oriented framework for addressing educational-management information challenges in Nigerian Colleges of Education and provides a conceptual foundation for subsequent prototype development and empirical evaluation.

items.title: Intelligent Systems for Space Conditioning and Shading in Buildings: A Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence Techniques and Their Energy Impact
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) control, whereas solar-radiation management still relies mainly on reactive strategies; whether AI capabilities validated in HVAC could be transferred to solar control has not been systematically assessed. This review compares both domains in terms of experimental maturity, climatic coverage, and input variables. Web of Science studies (2015–2026) reporting quantitative energy-demand variations were systematically reviewed following PRISMA 2020 and synthesized descriptively, with a sensitivity search adding reinforcement-learning and predictive-control terms. Fifty-six studies were included (29 HVAC, 28 solar, 1 shared). HVAC reductions ranged from 3.8% to 62.4% (median 22.1%), a spread associated more with heterogeneous baselines, durations, and metrics than with techniques. Real-world studies represented 31% in HVAC versus 14% in solar management, where AI-based predictive control appeared in one real-world study. Anticipatory variables were scarce but coincided with some of the highest savings, a non-causal association. Model-level patterns, such as Random Forest replication, were not preserved when 18 additional studies were considered. Transferring predictive control from HVAC to solar management is a promising line that requires long-term real-world validation in underrepresented climates. Limitations include a single database and single-reviewer screening. The review was not registered or externally funded.

This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of using interactive methods to develop reading comprehension skills in English language lessons. Particular attention is given to reciprocal teaching, jigsaw reading, think-pair-share, problem-based reading, guided questioning, and collaborative text analysis. The study draws on established approaches to reading instruction and research on interactive learning to explain how these methods can facilitate cognitive engagement, metacognitive awareness, learner autonomy, and communicative competence. items.title: IoT and AI-Based Approaches for Monitoring and Preventing Hazards from Inflammable Materials
items.abstract: Inflammable materials pose significant risks in industrial, residential, and transportation environments, often leading to catastrophic fire accidents and economic losses. Traditional hazard detection and safety management systems rely on manual monitoring or delayed response mechanisms, which limit their effectiveness. This research proposes an integrated approach using the Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for real-time monitoring, prediction, and prevention of hazards related to inflammable materials. IoT-based sensor networks were deployed to continuously track temperature, gas concentration, and environmental parameters, while AI algorithms analyzed the data to identify early warning signs of ignition risks. A hybrid machine learning model combining Support Vector Machines and Deep Neural Networks achieved high accuracy in hazard prediction, significantly reducing false alarms. Experimental simulations demonstrated that the proposed system improves response time and enhances overall safety. The findings suggest that the integration of IoT and AI can serve as a scalable, cost-effective solution for proactive fire prevention and risk management in industries handling inflammable substances.

items.title: IoT-Based Automatic Cotton Leaf Disease Detection, Infection Percentage Estimation, and Treatment Recommendation Using Raspberry PI
items.abstract: Cotton is one of the most important commercial crops worldwide, and its productivity is significantly affected by various leaf diseases such as bacterial blight, alter aria leaf spot, Cercospora leaf spot, powdery mildew, and leaf curl disease. Early and accurate identification of these diseases is essential to minimize crop losses and improve yield. Traditional disease diagnosis relies on manual field inspection by experts, which is time-consuming, labour-intensive, and often impractical for large agricultural fields. The proposed system integrates a Raspberry Pi5, a high-resolution camera module, environmental sensors, and wireless communication technologies to create an intelligent crop monitoring platform. Images of cotton leaves are captured using the Raspberry Pi camera and processed through computer vision techniques for leaf segmentation and feature extraction. A lightweight deep learning model based on MobileNetV2 is employed to automatically identify different cotton leaf diseases. In addition to disease classification, image segmentation techniques are used to calculate the percentage of infected leaf area, enabling the system to determine the severity level of infection. The system also collects environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, soil moisture, and light intensity using IoT sensors. These parameters, along with disease diagnosis results, are transmitted to a cloud-based dashboard for real-time monitoring and analysis. Automated alerts can be sent to farmers through SMS or mobile notifications when severe infections are detected. Experimental evaluation is expected to achieve disease classification accuracy above 93%, infection area estimation error below 5%, and real-time inference within one second per image on the Raspberry Pi platform. The proposed solution offers a cost-effective, portable, and scalable approach for precision agriculture by combining artificial intelligence, image processing, and IoT technologies. The system enables early disease detection, accurate infection assessment, timely treatment recommendations, reduced pesticide usage, and improved cotton crop productivity, making it a valuable tool for smart farming applications.

items.title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
items.abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

items.title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
items.abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

items.title: Knowledge Evolution and Paradigm-Level Change in AI-in-Education Research: A Scientometric Mapping and Critical Review (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. Two transition windows emerged. The weaker 2019–2020 window (Jensen–Shannon divergence, JSD = 0.058; retained under the permutation rule but not under a stricter interval-based rule) reflects a research-front transition toward learning analytics and prediction, accompanied by knowledge-base reconfiguration but no detectable change in teacher–learner roles. The 2022–2023 window (JSD = 0.187, the period maximum) coincides with the generative-AI surge and couples a newly formed co-citation community with a topic-specific rise in coagency whose direction is clear but whose magnitude is imprecisely estimated. Because these effects concentrate in 36.6% of the weighted corpus and recent citations remain right-censored, we classify the change, under our pre-specified labeling scheme, as localized paradigm-level reconfiguration rather than a field-level paradigm shift. The label is an operational classification within that scheme, not an independent determination that a paradigm shift has occurred.

items.title: Knowledge generation and evaluation for construction quality assessment using retrieval-augmented large language models
items.abstract: To address the problems of delayed knowledge updating, inefficient information acquisition, and difficulty in cross-project knowledge reuse in civil engineering construction quality assessment, this paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based methodology for injecting domain knowledge into large language models (LLMs). Multi-source knowledge, including national standards, journal articles, textbooks, and engineering reports, was systematically collected, cleaned, semantically segmented, and encoded using the bge-large-zh-v1.5 model to build a Milvus vector database. A general-purpose LLM was selected via semantic perplexity, and similarity-based retrieval was employed to construct prompt templates integrating role settings, prior knowledge, user queries, and response requirements, thereby enabling domain adaptation without additional training. An evaluation dataset containing 390 objective questions from registered architect and supervising engineer qualification examinations was constructed, and six representative LLMs along with their RAG-enhanced counterparts were evaluated. The results show that the average accuracy of general LLMs is 61.3%, with DeepSeek achieving the highest at 73.9%; after RAG enhancement, the accuracy rises to 86.3%, with significant improvements across all subjects. The proposed method effectively mitigates the hallucination phenomenon and provides traceable answers with source citations, enhancing both professionalism and interpretability, and offering a viable technical pathway for the digital transformation of the civil engineering industry.
